text: Aleister Crowley (/ˈælɪstər ˈkroʊli/; born Edward Alexander Crowley; 12 October 1875 – 1 December 1947) was an English occultist, ceremonial magician, poet, novelist, mountaineer, and painter. He founded the religion of Thelema, identifying himself as the prophet entrusted with guiding humanity into the Æon of Horus in the early 20th century. A prolific writer, he published widely over the course of his life. Born to a wealthy family in Royal Leamington Spa, Warwickshire, England, on 12 October 1875, Crowley was the son of Edward Crowley (1829–1887), an engineer who retired from a brewing business, and Emily Bertha Bishop (1848–1917), who came from a Devonshire-Somerset family and described her son as "the Beast," a name he embraced. The couple married in November 1874 at London's Kensington Registry Office and were evangelical Christians; Crowley's father converted to the Exclusive Brethren, a fundamentalist Christian group, and read a Bible passage to his wife and son daily after breakfast. After the death of their baby daughter in 1880, the family moved to Redhill, Surrey. At age 8, Crowley attended H. T. Habershon's evangelical Christian boarding school in Hastings and later Ebor preparatory school in Cambridge, run by Reverend Henry d'Arcy Champney, whom Crowley viewed as a sadist. In 1887, when Crowley was eleven, his father died of tongue cancer, an event he described as a turning point in his life and maintained an admiration for, calling him "my hero and my friend." Inheriting a third of his father's wealth, he began misbehaving at school and was punished harshly by Champney; his family removed him after he developed albuminuria. He then attended Malvern College and Tonbridge School, both of which he despised and left after a few terms. He became increasingly skeptical of Christianity, pointing out Biblical inconsistencies, and engaged in behaviors contrary to Christian morality, including smoking, masturbation, and having sex with prostitutes from whom he contracted gonorrhea. Sent to live with a Brethren tutor in Eastbourne, he took chemistry courses at Eastbourne College and developed interests in chess, poetry, and mountain climbing. In 1894, he climbed Beachy Head and visited the Alps, joining the Scottish Mountaineering Club. The following year, he climbed the Eiger, Trift, Jungfrau, Mönch, and Wetterhorn. He adopted the name Aleister over Edward, believing it fulfilled the ideal of a dactyl followed by a spondee, as in "Jeremy Taylor," and noted that Aleister is the Gaelic form of Alexander. In March 1896, while on holiday in Stockholm, Crowley had his first significant mystical experience, which several biographers, including Lawrence Sutin, Richard Kaczynski, and Tobias Churton, believe resulted from his first same-sex sexual experience, enabling him to recognize his bisexuality. At Cambridge, he maintained a vigorous sex life with women, mostly prostitutes, from one of whom he contracted syphilis, and eventually participated in same-sex activities despite their illegality. In October 1897, he met Herbert Charles Pollitt, president of the Cambridge University Footlights Dramatic Club, with whom he entered into a relationship; they broke apart because Pollitt did not share Crowley's growing interest in Western esotericism, a relationship Crowley regretted for years. In 1897, Crowley traveled to Saint Petersburg, Russia, intending to learn Russian for a future diplomatic career, but a brief illness in October 1897 triggered reflections on mortality and the futility of human endeavor, leading him to abandon diplomacy in favor of the occult. In March 1898, he obtained A. E. Waite's The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts and Karl von Eckartshausen's The Cloud upon the Sanctuary, furthering his occult interests. That same year, Leonard Smithers published 100 copies of Crowley's poem Aceldama: A Place to Bury Strangers In, which was not a success. He also published a string of other poems, including White Stains, a Decadent collection of erotic poetry printed abroad to avoid British prohibition. In July 1898, he left Cambridge without a degree, despite a "first class" showing in his 1897 exams and consistent "second class honours" results prior to that. In August 1898, he was in Zermatt, Switzerland, where he met chemist Julian L. Baker, with whom he discussed alchemy. Back in London, Baker introduced Crowley to George Cecil Jones, Baker's brother-in-law and a fellow member of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded in 1888. On 18 November 1898, Crowley was initiated into the Outer Order of the Golden Dawn at the Isis-Urania Temple in London's Mark Masons Hall by Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers, taking the magical motto and name "Frater Perdurabo," which he interpreted as "Brother I shall endure to the end." He moved into a luxury flat at 67–69 Chancery Lane and invited Allan Bennett, a senior Golden Dawn member, to live with him as his personal magical tutor. Bennett taught Crowley ceremonial magic and the ritual use of drugs, and together they performed Goetia rituals until Bennett left for South Asia to study Buddhism. In November 1899, Crowley purchased Boleskine House in Foyers on the shore of Loch Ness in Scotland, describing himself as the "Laird of Boleskine" and wearing traditional highland dress even in London. He continued writing poetry, publishing Jezebel and Other Tragic Poems, Tales of Archais, Songs of the Spirit, Appeal to the American Republic, and Jephthah in 1898–99; most received mixed reviews, though Jephthah was a critical success. Crowley progressed through the lower grades of the Golden Dawn and was ready for the inner Second Order, but was unpopular due to his bisexuality and libertine lifestyle, developing feuds with members including W. B. Yeats. When the London lodge refused to initiate him into the Second Order, he visited Mathers in Paris, who personally admitted him into the Adeptus Minor Grade. A schism had developed between Mathers and the London members, who were dissatisfied with his autocratic rule. Acting under Mathers' orders, Crowley, with the help of his mistress and fellow initiate Elaine Simpson, attempted to seize the Vault of the Adepts at 36 Blythe Road in West Kensington from the London lodge members. In court, the judge ruled in favor of the London lodge, as they had paid for the space's rent, leaving both Crowley and Mathers isolated from the group. In 1900, Crowley traveled to Mexico via the United States, settling in Mexico City and beginning a relationship with a local woman. He developed a love for the country, continued experimenting with ceremonial magic using John Dee's Enochian invocations, and later claimed to have been initiated into Freemasonry. He wrote a play based on Richard Wagner's opera Tannhäuser and a series of poems published as Oracles (1905). Eckenstein joined him in 1900, and together they climbed several mountains, including Iztaccihuatl, Popocatepetl, and Colima, which they had to abandon due to a volcanic eruption. Leaving Mexico, he went to San Francisco before sailing for Hawaii aboard the Nippon Maru, where he had a brief affair with a married woman named Mary Alice Rogers, whom he later wrote about in a series of poems published as Alice: An Adultery (1903). Briefly stopping in Japan and Hong Kong, Crowley reached Ceylon, where he met Allan Bennett, who was studying Shaivism. The pair spent time in Kandy before Bennett decided to become a Buddhist monk in the Theravada tradition and traveled to Burma. Crowley then toured India, devoting himself to the Hindu practice of Rāja yoga, believing he achieved the spiritual state of dhyana, and studied at the Meenakshi Temple in Madura. He also wrote poetry published as The Sword of Song (1904) and contracted malaria, recuperating in Calcutta and Rangoon. In 1902, he was joined in India by Eckenstein and several other mountaineers: Guy Knowles, H. Pfannl, V. Wesseley, and Jules Jacot-Guillarmod. Together, the Eckenstein-Crowley expedition attempted K2, which was never climbed, reaching an altitude of 20,000 feet (6,100 m) before turning back due to illness, including influenza, malaria, and snow blindness. In November 1902, he socialized with painter Gerald Kelly in Paris and became a fixture of the Parisian arts scene. While there, he wrote poems on sculptor Auguste Rodin, later published as Rodin in Rime (1907). W. Somerset Maugham, after briefly meeting Crowley, used him as a model for the character of Oliver Haddo in his novel The Magician (1908). He returned to Boleskine in April 1903 and, in August, married Gerald Kelly's sister Rose Edith Kelly in a "marriage of convenience" to prevent her from entering an arranged marriage; the marriage appalled the Kelly family and damaged his friendship with Gerald. On a honeymoon to Paris, Cairo, and then Ceylon, Crowley fell in love with Rose and wrote a series of love poems, published as Rosa Mundi and other Love Songs (1906), as well as authoring the religious satire Why Jesus Wept (1904). In February 1904, Crowley and Rose arrived in Cairo, where they pretended to be a prince and princess and rented an apartment in which Crowley set up a temple room to invoke ancient Egyptian deities while studying Islamic mysticism and Arabic. Rose regularly became delirious and informed him "they are waiting for you." On 18 March, she explained that "they" were the god Horus, and on 20 March proclaimed that "the Equinox of the Gods has come." She led him to a nearby museum, where she showed him a seventh-century BCE mortuary stele known as the Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu; Crowley believed the exhibit's number, 666, was significant as the "Number of the Beast" in Christian belief and later called it the "Stele of Revealing." According to Crowley's later account, on 8 April he heard a disembodied voice identifying itself as Aiwass, the messenger of Horus or Hoor-Paar-Kraat. He wrote down everything the voice told him over the next three days and titled it Liber AL vel Legis or The Book of the Law. The book proclaimed that humanity was entering a new Aeon and that Crowley would serve as its prophet, stating that a supreme moral law was "Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law," and that people should live in tune with their True Will. This book and its philosophy became the cornerstone of Thelema. Crowley said he was unsure what to do with The Book of the Law and often resented it, ignoring its commands, including taking the Stele of Revealing from the museum, fortifying his own island, and translating the book into all the world's languages. According to his account, he instead sent typescripts of the work to several occult groups.

On 8 April, Crowley heard a disembodied voice identifying itself as Aiwass, the messenger of Horus or Hoor-Paar-Kraat, and recorded everything the voice told him over the next three days, titling the work Liber AL vel Legis or The Book of the Law. The book declared that humanity was entering a new Aeon, with Crowley as its prophet, and introduced the supreme moral law "Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law," urging people to live in tune with their Will. This text and its philosophy became the foundation of Thelema. Crowley initially doubted the book's significance and often resented it, ignoring its commands, such as taking the Stele of Revealing from the museum, fortifying his island, and translating the book into all languages. Instead, he sent typescripts to known occultists, stored the manuscript, and neglected it. Returning to Boleskine, Crowley believed Mathers was using magic against him, leading to a breakdown in their relationship. On 28 July 1905, Rose gave birth to their first daughter, Lilith, and Crowley wrote the pornographic Snowdrops from a Curate's Garden to entertain his recovering wife. He founded a publishing company, the Society for the Propagation of Religious Truth, parodying the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, and published works like Crowley's Collected Works, edited by Ivor Back. His poetry received strong reviews but did not sell well; to gain publicity, he offered a £100 reward for the best essay on his work, won by J. F. C. Fuller, whose 1907 essay, The Star in the West, praised his poetry as among the greatest ever written. Crowley planned to climb Kanchenjunga in Nepal, the world's most treacherous mountain, but the expedition, involving Jacot-Guillarmod, Charles Adolphe Reymond, Alexis Pache, and Alcesti C. Rigo de Righi, was marred by conflict, with the others mutinying against his leadership as nightfall approached, resulting in the deaths of Pache and several porters, for which Crowley was widely blamed. In Moharbhanj, Crowley participated in big-game hunting and wrote The Scented Garden, a homoerotic work, before meeting Rose and Lilith in Calcutta and being forced to leave India after non-lethally shooting two men who attempted to mug him. He briefly visited Bennett in Burma, then toured southern China with his family, hiring porters and a nanny, smoking opium throughout the journey from Tengyueh to Yungchang, Tali, Yunnanfu, and Hanoi, and daily reciting the "Bornless Ritual" to invoke his Holy Guardian Angel. While Rose and Lilith returned to Europe, Crowley went to Shanghai to meet Elaine Simpson, who was fascinated by The Book of the Law; together they performed rituals to contact Aiwass. He then sailed to Japan and Canada before going to New York City, where he unsuccessfully sought support for a second Kanchenjunga expedition. Upon returning to Britain, he learned that his daughter Lilith had died of typhoid in Rangoon, which he later blamed on Rose's increasing alcoholism; under emotional distress, his health deteriorated, and he underwent several surgical operations. He began short-lived romances with actress Vera "Lola" Neville and author Ada Leverson; Lola Zaza was born in 1906, either in late summer, September, or the following winter, and contracted bronchitis and nearly died. With George Cecil Jones, Crowley continued performing the Abramelin rituals at the Ashdown Park Hotel in Coulsdon, Surrey, believing he attained samadhi or union with the Godhead, a turning point in his life. Using heavy amounts of hashish, he wrote "The Psychology of Hashish" (1909), championing the drug as a tool for mysticism. He claimed to have been contacted again by Aiwass in late October and November 1907, who dictated two additional texts, "Liber VII" and "Liber Cordis Cincti Serpente," later classified in Thelema's Holy Books. During the last two months of 1907, he wrote more Thelemic Holy Books, including "Liber LXVI," "Liber Arcanorum," "Liber Porta Lucis, Sub Figura X," "Liber Tau," "Liber Trigrammaton," and "Liber DCCCXIII vel Ararita," all received from a preternatural source. In June 1909, when the manuscript of The Book of the Law was rediscovered at Boleskine, he concluded that Thelema represented objective truth. His inheritance was dwindling; he was hired by George Montagu Bennett, the Earl of Tankerville, to protect him from witchcraft, recognizing Bennett's paranoia stemmed from cocaine addiction, and took him on holiday to France and Morocco. In 1907, he began taking paying students in occult and magical practice. Victor Neuburg, met in February 1907, became his sexual partner and closest disciple; in 1908, they toured northern Spain before going to Tangier, Morocco. The following year, Neuburg stayed at Boleskine, where they engaged in sadomasochism. Crowley continued writing prolifically, producing works such as Ambergris, Clouds Without Water, Konx Om Pax, and his first autobiography, The World's Tragedy, and wrote horror stories some of which were published, as well as articles in Vanity Fair, edited by Frank Harris. He also wrote Liber 777, a book of magical and Qabalistic correspondences borrowing from Mathers and Bennett. In November 1907, Crowley and Jones founded the A∴A∴, a successor to the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, aided by Fuller. The group's headquarters were at 124 Victoria Street in central London, with rites derived from the Golden Dawn but incorporating Thelemic elements. Early members included Richard Noel Warren, Austin Osman Spare, Horace Sheridan-Bickers, George Raffalovich, Francis Henry Everard Joseph Feilding, Herbert Edward Inman, Kenneth Ward, and Charles Stansfeld Jones. In March 1909, Crowley began publishing a biannual periodical, The Equinox, billed as "The Review of Scientific Illuminism," which became the "Official Organ" of the A∴A∴. Crowley grew increasingly frustrated with Rose's alcoholism and divorced her in November 1909 on grounds of his own adultery; Lola was placed in Rose's care, and the couple remained friends, with Rose continuing to live at Boleskine. Her alcoholism worsened, and she was institutionalized in September 1911. In November 1909, Crowley and Neuburg traveled to Algeria, touring from El Arba to Aumale, Bou Saâda, and Dā'leh Addin, with Crowley reciting the Quran to combat feelings of awe and dread. During the trip, he invoked the thirty aethyrs of Enochian magic, with Neuburg recording the results, later published in The Equinox as The Vision and the Voice. After a mountaintop sex magic ritual, he performed an evocation to the demon Choronzon involving blood sacrifice, which he considered a watershed in his magical career. Returning to London in January 1910, he found Mathers suing him for publishing Golden Dawn secrets in The Equinox; the court ruled in Crowley's favor, and the case gained widespread press coverage, increasing his fame. Crowley embraced the sensationalist image of being a Satanist and advocate of human sacrifice, despite neither being true. The publicity attracted new members to the A∴A∴, including Frank Bennett, James Bayley, Herbert Close, and James Windram. Leila Waddell soon became Crowley's lover. To expand his teachings, he developed the Rites of Artemis, a public performance of magic and symbolism featuring A∴A∴ members as deities, first performed at the A∴A∴ headquarters with attendees given fruit punch containing peyote; press reports were largely positive. In October and November 1910, he staged the Rites of Eleusis at Caxton Hall, Westminster, with mixed press reviews. West de Wend Fenton, editor of The Looking Glass, criticized Crowley as "one of the most blasphemous and cold-blooded villains of modern times," accusing him and Jones of homosexual activity; Crowley did not mind, but Jones sued for libel unsuccessfully, and Fuller broke off his friendship with Crowley. Crowley and Neuburg returned to Algeria for further magical workings. The Equinox continued publishing, and various books, including Ambergris, The Winged Beetle, The Scented Garden, Neuburg's The Triumph of Pan, and Ethel Archer's The Whirlpool, were published under its imprint. In 1911, Crowley and Waddell holidayed in Montigny-sur-Loing, where he wrote prolifically, producing poems, short stories, plays, and 19 works on magic and mysticism, including the two final Holy Books of Thelema. In Paris, he met Mary Desti, who became his next "Scarlet Woman," and they performed magical workings in St. Moritz; Crowley believed one of the Secret Chiefs, Ab-ul-Diz, spoke through her. Based on Desti's trance statements, he wrote the two-volume Book 4 (1912–13) and at the time developed the spelling "magick" to distinguish paranormal phenomena from stage magic. In early 1912, Crowley published The Book of Lies, described by biographer Lawrence Sutin as "his greatest success in merging his talents as poet, scholar, and magus." Theodor Reuss accused him of publishing O.T.O. secrets in The Book, but Crowley convinced Reuss the similarities were coincidental, and the two became friends. Reuss appointed Crowley head of O.T.O.'s British branch, the Mysteria Mystica Maxima (MMM), and at a Berlin ceremony, Crowley adopted the magical name Baphomet and was proclaimed "X° Supreme Rex and Sovereign Grand Master General of Ireland, Iona, and all the Britons." With Reuss's permission, Crowley advertised the MMM and rewrote many O.T.O. rituals, which were largely based on Freemasonry; the incorporation of Thelemite elements proved controversial. Fascinated by O.T.O.'s emphasis on sex magic, Crowley devised a magical working based on anal sex and included it in the syllabus for O.T.O. members initiated into the eleventh degree. In March 1913, Crowley acted as producer for The Ragged Ragtime Girls, a group of female violinists led by Waddell, performing at London's Old Tivoli theatre and later in Moscow for six weeks, where he had a sadomasochistic relationship with Hungarian Anny Ringler. In Moscow, he continued writing plays and poetry, including "Hymn to Pan" and the Gnostic Mass, a Thelemic ritual that became a key part of O.T.O. liturgy. Churton suggested Crowley had traveled to Moscow on orders of British intelligence to spy on revolutionary elements. In January 1914, Crowley and Neuburg settled in Paris, where Crowley was involved in the controversy over Jacob Epstein's monument to Oscar Wilde. Together, they performed the six-week "Paris Working," involving intense rituals and strong drug use, invoking Mercury and Jupiter, with acts of sex magic and journalist Walter Duranty present; inspired by the results, Crowley wrote Liber Agapé, a treatise on sex magic. After the Paris Working, Neuburg began distancing himself from Crowley, leading to an argument in which Crowley cursed him. By 1914, Crowley lived hand-to-mouth, relying on donations from A∴A∴ members and O.T.O. dues. In May, he transferred ownership of Boleskine House to the MMM for financial reasons, and in July he went mountaineering in the Swiss Alps, during which the First World War began. After recovering from phlebitis, he sailed for the United States aboard the RMS Lusitania in October 1914. Arriving in New York City, he moved into a hotel and began earning money writing for the American edition of Vanity Fair and doing freelance work for astrologer Evangeline Adams. In the city, he continued experimenting with sex magic using masturbation, female prostitutes, and male clients of a Turkish bathhouse, all documented in his diaries. Professing Irish ancestry and supporting Irish independence from Britain, Crowley began advocating for Germany in its war against Britain, becoming involved in New York's pro-German movement. In January 1915, pro-German propagandist George Sylvester Viereck employed him as a writer for The Fatherland, dedicated to keeping the U.S. neutral; in later years, detractors denounced him as a traitor to Britain. Crowley entered a relationship with Jeanne Robert Foster, touring the West Coast. In Vancouver, headquarters of the North American O.T.O., he met Charles Stansfeld Jones and Wilfred Talbot Smith to discuss Thelema's propagation on the continent. In Detroit, he experimented with peyote at Parke-Davis, then visited Seattle, San Francisco, Santa Cruz, Los Angeles, San Diego, Tijuana, and the Grand Canyon before returning to New York. There, he befriended Ananda Coomaraswamy and his wife Alice Richardson; they performed sex magic in April 1916, after which she became pregnant and then miscarried. Later that year, he took a "magical retirement" to a cabin by Lake Pasquaney owned by Evangeline Adams, where he used heavy drugs, performed a ritual, and proclaimed himself "Master Therion," writing short stories based on James George Frazer's The Golden Bough and a literary criticism work, The Gospel According to Bernard Shaw. In December, he moved to New Orleans, his favorite U.S. city, before spending February 1917 with evangelical Christian relatives in Titusville, Florida. Returning to New York City, he moved in with artist and A∴A∴ member Leon Engers Kennedy in May, learning of his mother's death. After The Fatherland collapsed, Crowley continued working with Viereck, who appointed him contributing editor of arts journal The International, which he used to promote Thelema before it ceased publication. He then moved to the studio apartment of Roddie Minor, who became his partner and Scarlet Woman; through their "Amalantrah Workings," he believed they were contacted by a preternatural entity named Lam. The relationship ended. In 1918, Crowley went on a magical retreat in the wilderness of Esopus Island on the Hudson River in upstate New York.

After undertaking a ritual, he proclaimed himself "Master Therion" and wrote several short stories based on James George Frazer's The Golden Bough and a literary criticism work, The Gospel According to Bernard Shaw. In December, he moved to New Orleans, his favorite U.S. city, before spending February 1917 with evangelical Christian relatives in Titusville, Florida. Returning to New York City, he moved in with artist and A∴A∴ member Leon Engers Kennedy in May, learning of his mother's death. After the collapse of The Fatherland, Crowley continued his association with Viereck, who appointed him contributing editor of the arts journal The International, where he promoted Thelema, though the journal soon ceased publication. He then moved to the studio apartment of Roddie Minor, who became his partner and Scarlet Woman; through their rituals, which Crowley called "The Amalantrah Workings," he believed they were contacted by a preternatural entity named Lam, a relationship that ended soon after. In 1918, Crowley went on a magical retreat on Esopus Island in upstate New York, where he began an adaptation of the Tao Te Ching, painted Thelemic slogans on riverside cliffs, and later claimed to experience past life memories of being Ge Xuan, Pope Alexander VI, Alessandro Cagliostro, and Éliphas Lévi. Back in New York City, he moved to Greenwich Village, where he took Leah Hirsig as his lover and next Scarlet Woman. He took up painting as a hobby, exhibiting at the Greenwich Village Liberal Club and attracting attention from The Evening World. With financial support from sympathetic Freemasons, Crowley revived The Equinox with the first issue of volume III, known as The Blue Equinox. He spent mid-1919 on a climbing holiday in Montauk, New York, before returning to London in December. Now destitute and back in London, Crowley faced attacks from the tabloid John Bull, which labeled him a traitorous "scum" for his work with the German war effort; though friends urged him to sue, he declined. When suffering from asthma, a doctor prescribed heroin, to which he soon became addicted. In January 1920, he moved to Paris, renting a house in Fontainebleau with Leah Hirsig; they were soon joined in a ménage à trois by Ninette Shumway and Leah's newborn daughter Anne "Poupée" Leah. Crowley had plans to form a Thelemite community called the Abbey of Thelema, inspired by the Abbaye de Thélème in François Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel. After consulting the I Ching, he chose Cefalù in Sicily as the location and began renting the old Villa Santa Barbara on 2 April. Moving to the commune with Hirsig, Shumway, and their children Hansi, Howard, and Poupée, Crowley described the situation as "perfectly happy ... my idea of heaven." They wore robes, performed rituals to the sun god Ra at set times, and occasionally conducted the Gnostic Mass; the rest of the day they followed their own interests. Crowley continued widespread correspondences, painted, wrote a commentary on The Book of the Law, and revised the third part of Book 4. He offered a libertine education for the children, allowing them to play all day and witness acts of sex magic. He occasionally traveled to Palermo to visit rent boys and buy supplies, including drugs; his heroin addiction dominated his life and cocaine eroded his nasal cavity. There was no cleaning rota, and wild dogs and cats wandered throughout the building, making it unsanitary. Poupée died in October 1920, and Ninette gave birth to a daughter, Astarte Lulu Panthea, shortly after. New followers continued to arrive at the Abbey, including film star Jane Wolfe, who arrived in July 1920, was initiated into the A∴A∴, and became Crowley's secretary; Cecil Frederick Russell, who disliked same-sex sexual magic and left after a year; and Frank Bennett, an Australian Thelemite who spent several months at the Abbey. In February 1922, Crowley returned to Paris for a retreat in an unsuccessful attempt to quit heroin. He then went to London to seek money, where he published articles in The English Review criticizing the Dangerous Drugs Act 1920 and wrote a novel, The Diary of a Drug Fiend, completed in July; the book received mixed reviews and was lambasted by the Sunday Express, which called for its burning and prevented further reprints. A young Thelemite, Raoul Loveday, moved to the Abbey with his wife Betty May; while Loveday was devoted to Crowley, May detested him and life at the commune, claiming Loveday was made to drink the blood of a sacrificed cat and required self-cutting with razors each time using the pronoun "I"; Loveday drank from a polluted stream, developed a liver infection, and died in February 1923. Returning to London, May told the press about her experience. John Bull proclaimed Crowley "the wickedest man in the world" and "a man we'd like to hang," and although Crowley considered many accusations slanderous, he could not afford legal fees to sue, so the attacks continued, spreading across Europe and North America. The Fascist government of Benito Mussolini learned of Crowley's activities and issued a deportation notice in April 1923, forcing him to leave Italy; without Crowley, the Abbey closed. Crowley and Hirsig went to Tunis, where, suffering from poor health, he unsuccessfully tried again to quit heroin and began writing his "autohagiography," The Confessions of Aleister Crowley. They were joined by Norman Mudd, who became Crowley's public relations consultant. Employing a local boy, Mohammad ben Brahim, as his servant, Crowley went with him on a retreat to Nefta, where they performed sex magic together. In January 1924, Crowley traveled to Nice, France, where he met Frank Harris, underwent a series of nasal operations, and visited the Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man, developing a positive opinion of its founder George Gurdjieff. Destitute, he took on a wealthy student, Alexander Zu Zolar, and later another American follower, Dorothy Olsen. Crowley took Olsen to Tunisia for a magical retreat in Nefta, where he also wrote To Man (1924), a declaration of his status as a prophet entrusted with bringing Thelema to humanity. After spending the winter in Paris, in early 1925 Crowley and Olsen returned to Tunis, where he wrote The Heart of the Master (1938) as an account of a vision from a trance. In March, Olsen became pregnant, and Hirsig was called to care for her; she miscarried, after which Crowley took Olsen back to France. Hirsig later distanced herself from Crowley, who then denounced her. According to Crowley, Reuss named him head of O.T.O. upon his death, but this was challenged by Heinrich Tränker, who called the Hohenleuben Conference in Thuringia, Germany, which Crowley attended; prominent members like Karl Germer and Martha Küntzel supported Crowley's leadership, while Albin Grau, Oskar Hopfer, and Henri Birven backed Tränker, resulting in a split in O.T.O. Moving to Paris, where he broke with Olsen in 1926, Crowley had numerous lovers over the following years with whom he experimented in sex magic. Throughout, he was plagued by poor health due to heroin and cocaine addictions. In 1928, Crowley met Israel Regardie, a young Englishman who embraced Thelema and became his secretary for three years; that year, he also met Gerald Yorke, who began organizing Crowley's finances but never became a Thelemite; he also befriended journalist Tom Driberg, who did not accept Thelema. It was in this period that Crowley published Magick in Theory and Practice, which received little attention at the time. In December 1928, he met the Nicaraguan Maria Teresa Sanchez (Maria Teresa Ferrari de Miramar). Crowley was deported from France by authorities who disliked his reputation and feared he was a German agent. To allow her to join him in Britain, he married Sanchez in August 1929. Now based in London, Mandrake Press agreed to publish his autobiography in a limited six-volume set, also publishing his novel Moonchild and the short story collection The Stratagem. Mandrake went into liquidation in November 1930, before the full set of The Confessions could be published. Mandrake's owner, P. R. Stephensen, wrote The Legend of Aleister Crowley, an analysis of media coverage surrounding him. In April 1930, Crowley moved to Berlin, where he took Hanni Jaegar as his magical partner; the relationship was troubled. In September, he went to Lisbon, Portugal, to meet poet Fernando Pessoa, where he decided to fake his own death, doing so with Pessoa's help at the Boca do Inferno rock formation. He then returned to Berlin, where he reappeared three weeks later at the opening of his art exhibition at the Gallery Neumann-Nierendorf. Crowley's paintings aligned with the fashion for German Expressionism; few sold, but press reports were largely favorable. In August 1931, he took Bertha Busch as his new lover; their relationship was violent and involved frequent physical assaults. He continued to have affairs with both men and women in the city and met notable figures such as Aldous Huxley and Alfred Adler. In January 1932, he took the communist Gerald Hamilton as a lodger, through whom he was introduced to figures in the Berlin far left; it is possible he was operating as a spy for British intelligence, monitoring the communist movement. Crowley left Busch and returned to London, where he took Pearl Brooksmith as his new Scarlet Woman. Undergoing further nasal surgery, in 1932 he was invited as guest of honor at Foyles' Literary Luncheon and by Harry Price to speak at the National Laboratory of Psychical Research. In need of money, he launched court cases against those he believed had libelled him; some were successful. He gained publicity in a lawsuit against Constable and Co for publishing Nina Hamnett's Laughing Torso (1932), which he alleged libeled him by calling his occult practices black magic, but lost the case. The case worsened his financial situation, and in February 1935 he was declared bankrupt. During the hearing, it was revealed that Crowley was spending three times his income for several years. Crowley developed a friendship with Deidre Patricia Doherty, who offered to bear his child, born in May 1937; named Randall Gair, Crowley nicknamed him Aleister Atatürk. He died in a car accident in 2002 at age 65. Crowley continued to socialize with friends, holding curry parties where he cooked particularly spicy food. In 1936, he published his first book in six years, The Equinox of the Gods, which contained a facsimile of The Book of the Law and was considered volume III, number 3 of The Equinox periodical; the work sold well and received a second print run. In 1937, he gave a series of public lectures on yoga in Soho. Crowley was now living largely off contributions from O.T.O.'s Agape Lodge in California, led by rocket scientist Jack Parsons. He was intrigued by the rise of Nazism in Germany and, influenced by his friend Martha Küntzel, believed Adolf Hitler might convert to Thelema; when the Nazis abolished the German O.T.O. and imprisoned Germer, who fled to the U.S., Crowley then criticized Hitler as a black magician. When the Second World War broke out, Crowley wrote to the Naval Intelligence Division offering his services, but they declined. He associated with various figures in Britain's intelligence community, including Dennis Wheatley, Roald Dahl, Ian Fleming, and Maxwell Knight, and wrote that he originated the "V for Victory" sign first used by the BBC; this has never been proven. In 1940, his asthma worsened and, with German-produced medication unavailable, he returned to using heroin, becoming addicted again. As the Blitz hit London, Crowley relocated to Torquay, where he was briefly hospitalized with asthma and entertained himself with visits to the local chess club. Tiring of Torquay, he returned to London, where he was visited by American Thelemite Grady McMurtry, to whom Crowley awarded the title of "Hymenaeus Alpha." He stipulated that Germer would be his immediate successor, but McMurty should succeed Germer after Germer's death. With O.T.O. initiate Lady Frieda Harris, Crowley developed plans to produce a tarot card set, designed by him and painted by Harris, accompanied by a book, The Book of Thoth, published in a limited edition by Chiswick Press in 1944. To aid the war effort, he wrote a proclamation on the rights of humanity, "Liber OZ," and a poem for the liberation of France, La Gauloise. Crowley's final publication during his lifetime was a book of poetry, Olla: An Anthology of Sixty Years of Song. Another project, Aleister Explains Everything, was posthumously published as Magick Without Tears. In April 1944, Crowley briefly moved to Aston Clinton in Buckinghamshire, where he was visited by poet Nancy Cunard, before relocating to Hastings in Sussex, where he took up residence at the Netherwood boarding house. He took a young man named Kenneth Grant as his secretary, paying him in magical teaching rather than wages. He was also introduced to John Symonds, whom he appointed as his literary executor; Symonds held little regard for Crowley and later published unfavorable biographies. Corresponding with illusionist Arnold Crowther, it was through him that Crowley was introduced to Gerald Gardner, the future founder of Gardnerian Wicca; they became friends, and Crowley authorized Gardner to revive Britain's ailing O.T.O. Another visitor was Eliza Marian Butler, who interviewed Crowley for her book The Myth of the Magus. Other friends and family also visited him, including Doherty and Crowley's son Aleister Atatürk. On 1 December 1947, Crowley died at Netherwood of chronic bronchitis aggravated by pleurisy and myocardial degeneration, aged 72. His funeral was held at Woodvale Crematorium, Brighton on 5 December; about a dozen people attended, and Louis Wilkinson read excerpts from the Gnostic Mass, The Book of the Law, and "Hymn to Pan." The funeral generated press controversy and was labeled a Black Mass by tabloids. Crowley's body was cremated; his ashes were sent to Karl Germer in the U.S., who buried them in his garden in Hampton, New Jersey. Crowley's belief system, Thelema, has been described by scholars as a religion, more specifically as a new religious movement and as a "magico-religious doctrine." Although The Book of the Law, composed in 1904, is its central text, Thelema developed as a complete system in the years after 1904. In his autobiography, Crowley wrote that his purpose in life was to "bring oriental wisdom to Europe and to restore paganism in a purer form," though what he meant by "paganism" was unclear.

Thelema, Crowley's belief system, has been described by scholars as a religion, a new religious movement, and a "magico-religious doctrine," with The Book of the Law (composed in 1904) serving as its central text, though the system fully developed in the years after 1904. In his autobiography, Crowley stated his purpose was to "bring oriental wisdom to Europe and to restore paganism in a purer form," though the meaning of "paganism" remained unclear. He also wrote in the 4th Book of Magick about a great pagan Umbral fleet ruled by Ottovius that would be passed to the great Spartan, a detail whose esoteric nature was unclear. His thought was influenced by diverse sources, including eastern religious traditions like Hindu yoga and Buddhism, scientific naturalism, and Western esotericism such as ceremonial magic, alchemy, astrology, Rosicrucianism, Kabbalah, and the Tarot. He was deeply influenced by the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, though he expanded upon their teachings with his own interpretations. Crowley incorporated concepts from South Asian traditions like yoga and Tantra into Thelema, believing in a fundamental resemblance between Western and Eastern spiritual systems. Historian Alex Owen noted that Crowley followed the "modus operandi" of the Decadent movement throughout his life. Crowley believed the twentieth century marked the beginning of the Aeon of Horus, a new era in which humans would take greater control of their destiny, following the Aeon of Osiris (dominated by paternalistic religions like Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism) and the Aeon of Isis (maternalistic and goddess-centered). He considered Thelema to be the proper religion of the Aeon of Horus and saw himself as its prophet. Thelema centers on the idea that each person has a True Will that should be discovered and pursued, in harmony with the Cosmic Will. This process, referred to as "the Great Work" or the attainment of the "knowledge and conversation of the Holy Guardian Angel," was achieved through the Abramelin operation, a ceremonial magic ritual from a 17th-century grimoire. The moral code "Do What Thou Wilt" is regarded by Thelemites as the religion's ethical law, though historian Marco Pasi noted it was not anarchistic or libertarian, as Crowley viewed individuals as part of a larger societal organism. Crowley believed in the objective existence of magic, which he spelled as "Magick," an archaic form of the word. In Magick in Theory and Practice, he defined Magick as "the Science and Art of causing change to occur in conformity with Will." He told his disciple Karl Germer that "Magick is getting into communication with individuals who exist on a higher plane than ours. Mysticism is the raising of oneself to their level." He saw Magick as a third way between religion and science, giving The Equinox the subtitle "The Method of Science; the Aim of Religion." He expressed positive views toward science and the scientific method, urging magicians to keep detailed records of their experiments, stating, "The more scientific the record is, the better." His understanding of magic was influenced by James Frazer, particularly the idea that magic preceded science in cultural evolution, though unlike Frazer, Crowley did not see magic as a relic to be eradicated, but rather as a force to be adapted to the new age of science. In his alternative framework, old systems of magic declined so that science and magic could synthesize into magick, which would accept both the supernatural and an experimental method. Crowley adopted a broad definition of magick that included almost all forms of technology, using an instrumentalist view of magic, science, and technology. To Crowley, the greatest aim of the magician was to merge with a higher power connected to the wellsprings of the universe, though he never consistently defined that power—sometimes as God, the One, a goddess, or one's own Holy Guardian Angel or higher self—and ultimately accepted that the nature of divinity remained a mystery. As a result, he wrote at times like an atheist, at times like a monotheist, and at other times like a polytheist. Sexuality played a central role in Crowley's ideas about magick and practice, and is described as central to Thelema. He outlined three forms of sex magick—autoerotic, homosexual, and heterosexual—and argued such acts could focus a magician's will on specific goals like financial gain or creative success. For Crowley, sex was a sacrament, with the consumption of sexual fluids interpreted as a Eucharist, often manifested through the Cakes of Light—a biscuit containing menstrual blood or a mixture of semen and vaginal fluids. The Gnostic Mass is the central religious ceremony in Thelema. Crowley's theological beliefs were inconsistent; historian Ronald Hutton noted that some writings suggest atheism, others polytheism, and others mystical monotheism. Based on The Book of the Law, Crowley described a pantheon of three deities from ancient Egypt: Nuit, Hadit, and Ra-Hoor-Khuit, and in 1928 stated all true deities derived from this trinity. Jason Josephson Storm argued that Crowley synthesized Christian theology and Neopaganism, drawing on 19th-century works like Frazer's Golden Bough, while remaining critical of institutional Christianity. Crowley did not consider himself a Satanist nor did he worship Satan, rejecting the Christian worldview in which Satan exists. He used Satanic imagery, such as describing himself as "the Beast 666" and referring to the Whore of Babylon, and sent "Antichristmas cards" to friends. In some writings, he identified Aiwass as Satan and called him "Our Lord God the Devil." Scholar Gordon Djurdjevic stated that Crowley was "emphatically not" a Satanist, "if for no other reason than simply because he did not identify himself as such." Crowley expressed strong anti-Christian sentiment, stating he hated Christianity "as Socialists hate soap," likely stemming from his experiences with the Plymouth Brethren. He was influenced by the King James Bible, especially the Book of Revelation, and was accused of advocating human sacrifice due to a passage in Book 4 stating that "a male child of perfect innocence and high intelligence is the most satisfactory victim" and that he had sacrificed about 150 annually—a tongue-in-cheek reference to ejaculation, not understood by critics. Crowley considered himself one of the outstanding figures of his time. Hutton described him as a self-indulgent, flamboyant young man who deliberately flouted social and religious norms, shielded from public outrage by his inherited wealth. Hutton also noted his "unappeasable desire" to control organizations and his "tendency to quarrel savagely" with challengers. Biographer Martin Booth described Crowley as "self-confident, brash, eccentric, egotistic, highly intelligent, arrogant, witty, wealthy, and, when it suited him, cruel." Richard B. Spence noted he was "capable of immense physical and emotional cruelty." Biographer Lawrence Sutin described him as showing "courage, skill, dauntless energy, and remarkable focus of will" alongside "blind arrogance, petty fits of bile, [and] contempt for the abilities of his fellow men." Thelemite Lon Milo DuQuette noted that Crowley "was by no means perfect" and "often alienated those who loved him dearest." Crowley enjoyed being outrageous and flouting conventional morality, with John Symonds noting he was "in revolt against the moral and religious values of his time." His political thought was studied by Marco Pasi, who found that socio-political concerns were subordinate to metaphysical and spiritual ones. He was neither on the left nor right but is best categorized as a "conservative revolutionary," despite not being affiliated with the German movement of the same name. Pasi noted Crowley's fascination with Nazism and Marxism–Leninism due to their anti-Christian stance and revolutionary potential, seeing in them the possibility of destroying old religious traditions and creating a void for Thelema to fill. He described democracy as an "imbecile and nauseating cult of weakness" and cited The Book of the Law stating "there is the master and there is the slave; the noble and the serf; the 'lone wolf' and the herd," influenced by Social Darwinism and Friedrich Nietzsche. Although he had contempt for most of the British aristocracy, he regarded himself as an aristocrat and styled himself as Laird Boleskine, once describing his ideology as "aristocratic communism." Crowley was bisexual but preferred women, with relationships with men being fewer and mostly early in life. He was particularly attracted to "exotic women," and stated he fell in love multiple times; Kaczynski noted that when he loved, he did so with his whole being, though the passion was typically short-lived. Even in later life, he attracted young bohemian women due to his charisma. He applied the term "Scarlet Woman" to female lovers he believed played an important role in his magical work. During homosexual acts, he usually played the passive role, which Booth believed appealed to his masochistic side. A recurring theme in his writings is that spiritual enlightenment arises through transgressing socio-sexual norms. Crowley advocated complete sexual freedom for both men and women, arguing that homosexual and bisexual people should not suppress their orientation, stating that a person "must not be ashamed or afraid of being homosexual if he happens to be so at heart; he must not attempt to violate his own true nature because of public opinion, or medieval morality, or religious prejudice which would wish he were otherwise." On other issues, he adopted a more conservative stance, opposing abortion on moral grounds, believing no woman following her True Will would desire one. Biographer Lawrence Sutin stated that "blatant bigotry is a persistent minor element in Crowley's writings." He described Crowley as a "spoiled scion of a wealthy Victorian family" who embodied many of the worst John Bull racial and social prejudices of his time, noting the contradiction between societal racism and fascination with people of color. Crowley insulted his close Jewish friend Victor Neuburg with antisemitic slurs and held mixed opinions about Jewish people as a group, praising their "sublime" poetry and qualities like imagination, romance, loyalty, probity, and humanity, while also claiming centuries of persecution led some to exhibit "avarice, servility, falseness, cunning and the rest." He praised the Chinese for exhibiting "spiritual superiority" over the English and Muslims for showing "manliness, straightforwardness, subtlety, and self-respect." Critics and adherents of Thelema have accused Crowley of sexism. Booth described him as exhibiting "general misogyny," which the biographer attributed to a bad relationship with his mother. Sutin noted that Crowley largely accepted the Victorian notion of women as secondary in intellect and sensibility. Scholar Manon Hedenborg White noted that some of Crowley's statements are "undoubtedly misogynist by contemporary standards," though characterized his attitude as complex and multi-faceted. His views on women varied dramatically in his writings. He described women as "moral inferiors" who needed to be treated with "firmness, kindness and justice," while also arguing that Thelema was essential to women's emancipation. Biographers Richard B. Spence and Tobias Churton have suggested that Crowley was a spy for British secret services, claiming he joined the Golden Dawn under their direction to monitor Mathers, who was a Carlist. Spence suggested the conflict between Mathers and the London lodge was part of an intelligence operation to undermine Mathers' authority. He proposed that Crowley's trip to Mexico was to explore Mexican oil prospects for British intelligence and that his trip to China was part of a British scheme to monitor the opium trade. Churton suggested that Crowley traveled to Moscow at the orders of British intelligence to spy on revolutionary elements. Spence and Sutin both wrote that Crowley's pro-German work in the United States during World War I was a cover for being a double agent for Britain, citing his hyperbolic articles in The Fatherland to make the German lobby appear ridiculous to Americans. Spence also wrote that Crowley encouraged the German Navy to destroy the Lusitania, informing them it would keep the US out of the war, while in reality hoping it would bring the US into the war on Britain's side. Today, Crowley is regarded as a source of inspiration by many seeking spiritual enlightenment or magical practice. While his books sold poorly and his disciples were few during his lifetime, his important works are now constantly in print, and the number of self-identified "thelemites" worldwide is several thousand. His influence on magically oriented new religious movements has been deep and pervasive; understanding aspects of Anglo-Saxon neo-paganism and contemporary satanism requires knowledge of Crowley's doctrines. In poetry, alpinism, and painting, he may have been a minor figure, but in the context of occultism, he has played and continues to play a major role. Crowley remains an influential figure among occultists and in popular culture, particularly in Britain and other parts of the world. In 2002, a BBC poll ranked him 73rd in a list of the 100 Greatest Britons. Richard Cavendish wrote that "In native talent, penetrating intelligence and determination, Aleister Crowley was the best-equipped magician to emerge since the seventeenth century." Scholar Egil Asprem described him as "one of the most well-known figures in modern occultism."

Crowley's influence spans several thousands of people worldwide and has been deeply and pervasively embedded in magically oriented new religious movements, making it difficult to understand aspects of Anglo-Saxon neo-paganism and contemporary satanism without a solid grasp of his doctrines. While he may have been a minor figure in poetry, alpinism, and painting, within the context of occultism, he has played and continues to play a major role. He remains a significant figure among occultists and in popular culture, especially in Britain, but also globally; in 2002, a BBC poll ranked him 73rd in a list of the 100 Greatest Britons. Richard Cavendish described Crowley as the best-equipped magician since the seventeenth century in terms of native talent, penetrating intelligence, and determination. Egil Asprem called him one of the most well-known figures in modern occultism, while Wouter Hanegraaff viewed him as an extreme representation of "the dark side of the occult" and the most notorious occultist magician of the twentieth century. John Moore regarded Crowley as a "Modern Master" compared to figures like George Gurdjieff, P. D. Ouspensky, Rudolf Steiner, and Helena Blavatsky, and described him as a "living embodiment" of Oswald Spengler's "Faustian Man." Biographer Tobias Churton saw Crowley as a pioneer of consciousness research, Hutton noted his important role in the modern Western response to Oriental spiritual traditions, and Sutin acknowledged his distinct original contributions to the study of yoga in the West. After his death, Thelema continued to develop; in 1969, the O.T.O. was reactivated in California under Grady Louis McMurtry, and in 1985, its title was unsuccessfully challenged in court by the Society Ordo Templi Orientis, led by Marcelo Ramos Motta. Kenneth Anger, an American filmmaker, was influenced by Crowley's writings from a young age. In the UK, Kenneth Grant promoted Typhonian Thelema through the Typhonian O.T.O., later renamed the Typhonian Order. Amado Crowley claimed to be Crowley's son and argued that Thelema was a false religion created to conceal Crowley's true teachings, a claim refuted by academic investigation. Djurdjevic stated that Crowley's influence on twentieth-century and contemporary esotericism has been enormous. Gerald Gardner, the founder of Gardnerian Wicca, used much of Crowley's published material in composing the Gardnerian ritual liturgy, and Rosaleen Norton was also heavily influenced by Crowley. Crowley became a dominant figure in the modern Pagan community. L. Ron Hubbard, founder of Scientology, engaged with Thelema in the early 1940s through Jack Parsons, and it has been argued that Crowley's ideas influenced some of Hubbard's work. Asbjørn Dyrendel, James R. Lewis, and Jesper Petersen noted that despite not being a Satanist, Crowley embodies the pre-Satanist esoteric discourse on Satan and Satanism through his lifestyle and philosophy, with his "image and ought" becoming an important influence on religious Satanism, notably affecting figures like Anton LaVey and Michael Aquino. Following his time in Cefalù, various "literary Crowleys" emerged in fiction: Shelley Arabin in John Buchan's 1926 novel The Dancing Floor, Damien Mocata in Dennis Wheatley's The Devil Rides Out, characters in Dion Fortune's The Secrets of Doctor Taverner (1926) and The Winged Bull (1935), and Dr. Trelawney in Anthony Powell's A Dance to the Music of Time. Crowley appeared on the cover art of The Beatles' 1967 album Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, and his motto "Do What Thou Wilt" was inscribed on the vinyl of Led Zeppelin's 1970 album Led Zeppelin III. Jimmy Page, co-founder of Led Zeppelin, bought Boleskine in 1971, part of the band's film The Song Remains the Same was filmed there, and he sold it in 1992. David Bowie referenced Crowley and his works in songs such as After All, "Quicksand" (1971), Station To Station, and it has been suggested that the lyrics of his 1983 hit "Let's Dance" substantially paraphrase Crowley's 1923 poem "Lyric of Love to Leah." Ozzy Osbourne and lyricist Bob Daisley wrote a song titled "Mr. Crowley" in 1980. A prophetic quote from Crowley's Magick in Theory and Practice (1911) was used as the opening introduction to the video game Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain (1996). Crowley began to receive scholarly attention from academics in the late 1990s.
